question: Why does the second derivative test tell you whether a critical point is a minimum or a saddle?

turns.response:
{"topic": "Second Derivative Test (multivariable, via the Hessian)",
"summary": "At a critical point the gradient vanishes, so the local shape is governed by the quadratic form built from the Hessian matrix $H$. If $H$ is positive definite the surface curves up in every direction (a minimum); if its eigenvalues have mixed signs it curves up one way and down another (a saddle). The determinant/eigenvalue signs just encode which case you are in.",

"disciplines": ["calculus", "linear-algebra"],
"beats": [
  {"title": "Flat where the gradient dies", "claim": "At a critical point the tangent plane is horizontal, so first derivatives give no info about min vs saddle."},
  {"title": "Zoom in on the bowl", "claim": "Near the critical point the function is well-approximated by the quadratic form (1/2) xᵀHx from its Taylor expansion."},
  {"title": "Curvature lives in the Hessian", "claim": "The second-derivative matrix H measures how the surface bends in each direction."},
  {"title": "Eigenvectors are the pure directions", "claim": "The eigenvectors of H are the axes along which the surface bends independently; eigenvalues are those bending rates."},
  {"title": "Two ups make a bowl", "claim": "Both eigenvalues positive means curvature up everywhere — H positive definite — a local minimum."},
  {"title": "One up, one down: saddle", "claim": "Mixed-sign eigenvalues mean up along one axis and down along another, producing a saddle."},
  {"title": "Determinant reads the signs", "claim": "det H = product of eigenvalues, so det<0 forces mixed signs (saddle); det>0 with f_xx>0 forces both positive (min)."}
]}
